description: We are Fibonauci Team, a team of curious minds, creative thinkers, and aspiring innovators passionate about space exploration, science, and technology.
summary:
Still Out There is an animated crayon storybook about the machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, made for school-age space enthusiasts as a NASA hackathon entry by Team Fibonacci.

Kit, a new Signal Keeper, and their robot Echo pick up a faint message from Voyager 1. It asks them to visit the explorers that went first, including Surveyor 3, the Apollo lunar module and rover, Viking, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Ingenuity, Kepler and the Pioneers. Across 44 hand-drawn, gently animated spreads, readers tap 16 playful moments, like landing Surveyor, firing a laser at the Moon, flying Ingenuity or decoding the Pioneer plaque. At the end, they write a message back to Voyager.

Each page has three reading layers: a big Spark line, a short Story and a Mission Log of facts, all drawn from NASA and NSSDCA sources. It saves progress, reads aloud, offers calm-motion and text-size settings, and works with keyboard, mouse and touch. Accessibility scores are Lighthouse 100 and zero axe issues on tested screens.

Built with React, React Three Fiber, Zustand and Vite, and tested with Playwright and Vitest. Not affiliated with NASA.
details:
Still Out There is an animated crayon storybook about the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It was built by Team Fibonacci, under the guidance of FreeFall-labs, as an entry to a NASA hackathon challenge: tell the story of these machines for school-age space enthusiasts. Most of their histories live in dense technical pages and textbooks, so the team set out to tell them as stories instead. The live version runs in any browser on phone, tablet or laptop.

The story. Kit, a new Signal Keeper, and their little robot Echo pick up a faint message from Voyager 1, the farthest machine people have ever built. Voyager asks them to visit the explorers that went first, and the radio signal works like a door into each explorer's memory. Kit and Echo appear in every scene as glowing visitors in little space helmets. The book runs 44 spreads across seven parts:

  • Prologue: Voyager 1.
  • The Moon: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle, the laser reflector, the Apollo 12 science station and the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle.
  • Mars, The First Visitors: Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder with Sojourner, and Phoenix.
  • Mars, The Long Drivers: Spirit and Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity and Perseverance.
  • Small Worlds: NEAR Shoemaker on Eros, and Dawn at Vesta and Ceres.
  • Beyond: Kepler, and Pioneer 10 and 11.
  • Finale, One Light-Day: Voyager again, where the reader writes a message back and watches it travel the 24 hours to reach it.

Each explorer tells its own story in its own words, with real facts and dates. NASA hardware keeps its real shape and never gets a face. It speaks through speech panels and a gentle glow.

The experience. Every page is a layered scene with soft parallax, a hand-drawn "line boil", painted shadows and paper grain. Readers can tap 16 playful moments drawn from the script, such as landing Surveyor 3 with Engine off!, bouncing a laser off the Moon, steering a rover under a dust devil, releasing the airbags, flying Ingenuity, landing NEAR gently, spotting a planet's dip in starlight and decoding the Pioneer plaque. Scenes made in code add Viking's first picture building up stripe by stripe, Mars cut open to show crust, mantle and core, and a glowing marker in the sky for each explorer. Nothing can be failed, so young readers can explore freely. Slower, dimmer "quiet pages" handle the goodbyes, such as Opportunity's last dust storm.

Three reading layers. A big Spark line suits young readers, a short Story suits most readers, and a Mission Log of extra facts behind a tap serves teens, adults and the curious.

Features and accessibility. The book saves your place and settings on your device. Continue picks up where you left off, and Start over asks first. A speaker button reads each page aloud where the browser supports speech. Settings cover sound, music volume, calm motion, three text sizes and read-aloud. It scores 100 on Lighthouse accessibility and has zero axe (WCAG 2.1 A and AA) issues on the cover, Settings, Credits, the chapter menu and 10 representative pages. It works fully by keyboard with visible focus rings, and Escape closes cards. Every scene has a text description, and each page's words are announced to screen readers. Reduced motion follows the device setting or can be switched on manually. Touch targets are at least 44 px, and all text meets WCAG AA contrast.

Accuracy. Every fact comes from a verified storyline based on NASA and NSSDCA mission pages, with sources listed by chapter on the Credits screen. Pages in the first person are told from the explorer's point of view, but the facts in them are real. Voyager's lines about reaching one light-day from Earth change on November 18, 2026, the day it happens.

Under the hood. The app is built with Vite and React. React Three Fiber (three.js, drei and postprocessing) renders the animated layered scenes with depth of field and a vignette, and Zustand stores progress and settings in the browser. Vitest covers the date-aware Voyager text. Playwright with axe-core handles review screenshots, accessibility checks and end-to-end checks, including all 16 tap moments, saving behavior, and speech-bubble layout on every page at three screen sizes. Sharp prepares the art by converting it to WebP and cleaning sprite edges. Story content is built from the script by a build script, so the text stays word-for-word faithful to the source.

Credits. Interface sounds and emotes are by Kenney (CC0), the font is Fredoka under the SIL Open Font License, and the layer shader is based on work by Gianmarco Simone. The project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

The closing line sums up the book: "They're quiet now. But they're still out there. And so is the next explorer: you."
